Gastric glands consist of multicellular peptic glands secreting a pro-enzyme called pepsinogen and unicellular oxyntic cells secreting hydrochloric acid. The gastric juice secreted by the gastric glands contains a large amount of water, inactive pepsinogen enzyme and hydrochloric acid. Inactive pepsinogen changes into active pepsin, if mixed with hydrochloric acid (HCl). Pepsinogen secreted by oesophagus also becomes active by HCl in stomach. Hydrochloric acid prevents the bacterial decomposition and dissolves the inorganic salts as well as makes the food soft. The pepsin acts on proteins of food and changes them into peptones and proteoses.

Pepsin + Proteins → Peptones + Proteoses Now, Food takes the form of a thick creamy acidic fluid called chyme. Peristalsis in the stomach wall forces the chyme to pass in small amount at a time through the pyloric opening into the duodenum. To conclude, three functions of stomach are: Storage of food, mechanical mixing and chemical modification of food. iii. Intestinal Digestion: As the acidic chyme enters duodenum, wall of duodenum is also stimulated and secretes two hormones namely secretin and cholecystokinin which diffuse into the blood and reach the pancreas and liver respectively. Then, secretin stimulates the pancreas to secrete pancreatic juice and cholecystokinin activates the gall bladder to release the bile juice.

Bile and pancreatic juices are poured into the duodenum through the common hepatopancreatic duct. Meanwhile, the intestinal mucosa layer also secretes the intestinal juice called succus entericus under the influence of enterocrinin hormone. All the three substances get mixed up with the food in the intestine.

Bile contains no digestive enzymes. It is alkaline because it contains certain inorganic salts like sodium bicarbonate, sodium glycocholate and sodium taurocholate which not only neutralise the acidity of the chyme but also activates pancreatic juice as the pancreatic juice acts only in alkaline medium. Bile juice mechanically breaks down larger fat into small globules, called emulsification.

Pancreatic Juice contains powerful enzymes such as amylase (amylopsin), trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen and lipase (steapsin). All of them act in alkaline medium and hydrolyse carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Trypsinogen is an inactive enzyme or pro-enzyme and gets activated by enterokinase enzyme found in succus entericus. Trypsin is also called autocatalyst as it activates more trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen to form trypsin and chymotrypsin respectively.
Trypsin and chymotrypsin acts on proteins, peptones and proteoses hydrolysing them into simple amino acids.
Amylase acts on starches changing them into maltose, and lipase acts on emulsified fat to form fatty acids and glycerol.

Trypsinogen (inactive) + Enterokinase → Trypsin (active) Trypsin + Protein + proteoses and peptones → Smaller polypeptides + Amino acids Amylopsin + Starch → Maltose (Disaccharides) Steapsin + Emulsified fats → Fatty acids + Glycerol.
Succus Entericus is also an alkaline fluid containing many enzymes such as enterokinase, peptidases (erepsin), lipase, maltase, sucrase (invertase), lactase, ribonuclease and deoxyribonuclease.

Peptidases + Polypeptides → Aminoacids Lipase + Emulsified fat → fatty acid and glycerol Maltase +maltose → glucose + glucose Sucrase + sucrose → glucose + fructose Lactase+ lactose → glucose + galactose Similarly, Ribo-nuclease and deoxyribonuclease change the nucleic acids into nucleotides which are used in the synthesis of DNA, RNAand ATP. In this way, food is thoroughly digested with the help of enzymes. Consequently, all the proteins are changed into amino acids, carbohydrates into glucose and simple sugars and fats into glycerol and fatty acids.
